title: The Use of Spies
sourceOrigin: Project Gutenberg eBook #17405, The Art of War by Sunzi, Lionel Giles translation, 1910, public domain

approvedQuoteLedger.text: What enables the wise sovereign and the good general to strike and conquer, and achieve things beyond the reach of ordinary men, is foreknowledge.
Knowledge of the enemy's dispositions can only be obtained from other men.
Spies are a most important element in war, because on them depends an army's ability to move.

structureSummary.part1: sentences 1-3: opening economic argument — cost of armies versus cost of intelligence
structureSummary.part2: sentences 4-6: foreknowledge as the decisive differentiator; rejected sources (spirits, experience, calculation); human sources only
structureSummary.part3: sentences 7-13: five spy classes defined (local, inward, converted, doomed, surviving)
structureSummary.part4: sentence 8: divine manipulation of threads — all five types operating simultaneously
structureSummary.part5: sentences 14-19: management requirements for spies (sagacity, liberality, secrecy)
structureSummary.part6: sentences 20-25: converted spy as the hinge — enables all other types; treated with utmost liberality
structureSummary.part7: sentences 26-27: historical precedent (I Chih, Lü Ya) and closing claim — spies are most important element in war
